title: Probabilities & the sigmoid function
intro: So far logistic regression made hard predictions: this class, or that. But under the hood sits a beautiful mechanism that turns the raw model output into a genuine probability — and that immediately explains when the model is "sure of itself". Here you'll find the sigmoid formula, what exp() actually does, and why the S-curve pops up everywhere: from logistic regression to neural networks.

sections.title: From decision boundary to probability map

blocks.html: In chapter 1 we saw decision-boundary pictures with coloured regions: wherever the fill has a colour, that class is predicted. Make the same picture but now colour it by the predicted probability of the red class and a rolling landscape appears: on the decision boundary the probability is exactly 0.5; further away from the boundary it becomes ever redder (towards 1) or bluer (towards 0). More than 50% sure it is red → predict red; otherwise blue. The hard decision boundary and the probability map are thus two sides of the same coin.

In those probability figures regularisation was almost switched off (very large C). Turn regularisation on and the probabilities hug 0.5 more closely — smaller coefficients mean less confident predictions. See the connection: overconfidence ↔ overfitting.

sections.title: The sigmoid: from any number to [0, 1]

blocks.html: How are those probabilities computed? From the raw model output (the score \( z = w \cdot x + b \) from the logistic regression pipeline), which can itself be any real number — while probabilities live between 0 and 1. So we need something that "squeezes" the raw output into that interval: the sigmoid function. Study the curve below and slide along: at raw output zero the probability is 0.5 (exactly on the boundary); at positive raw output the probability of the positive class approaches 1; at negative output it approaches 0 — in other words: strong confidence in the negative class. Because the raw output grows the further you sit from the boundary, you are also more confident there.

blocks.label: sigmoid function
blocks.latex: \sigma(z) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P(y = 1 \mid x) \;=\; \sigma\bigl( w \cdot x + b \bigr)
blocks.caption: The sigmoid squeezes any raw output into (0, 1) — this is the probability that the example belongs to the positive class.

blocks.title: The sigmoid function
blocks.subtitle: Drag z: the yellow dot runs along the curve while σ(z) and exp(−z) are recomputed live. At z = 0, σ = 0.5 — exactly on the decision boundary.

rows: exactly on the decision boundary the probability is half
symmetry: as far left of the boundary as right, but flipped
never exactly 0 or 1 — only ever closer
a larger raw output always gives a larger probability
slow start, fast through the middle, saturating at the ends

blocks.html: Why is the threshold 0.5 and not something else? Because σ(z) ≥ 0.5 is exactly the same as z ≥ 0: the threshold hides inside the sign of the raw output. That is why predict() in logistic regression simply checks whether the score is positive.

sections.title: exp(): the engine under the sigmoid

blocks.html:
The denominator of the sigmoid holds \( e^{-z} \) — and that exp() is more than a stray magic symbol. The base e is Euler's number (±2.71828…) and exp(z) means nothing more than e multiplied by itself z times: \( \exp(1) = e \), \( \exp(2) = e \cdot e \), \( \exp(0) = 1 \). Why this particular base? Because e is the natural base of continuous growth: wherever an increase is proportional to the current amount (interest on interest, population growth, cooling coffee, radioactive decay), the quantity naturally grows or shrinks by a factor e per unit of time. That is why exp shows up all over science.

Three properties carry the sigmoid: (1) \( e^0 = 1 \) — hence \( \sigma(0) = \frac{1}{1+1} = 0.5 \); (2) \( \exp(-z) = 1/\exp(z) \) — negative powers are simply the reciprocal; (3) \( \exp \) grows faster than any polynomial yet shrinks towards zero without ever reaching it. Inside the sigmoid, \( e^{-z} \) therefore acts as a brake: every extra unit of z multiplies that brake by 1/e (±0.37). Large z → brake ≈ 0 → \( \sigma \approx 1/(1+0) = 1 \). Negative z → the brake explodes (at \( z = -5 \) it is already \( e^5 \approx 148 \)) → \( \sigma \approx 0 \).

Read the table as a ride along the decision boundary: on the left (negative score) the brake is large and the probability small; at the boundary the brake is exactly 1 and the probability 0.5; on the right the brake slams shut and the probability approaches 1. Note the symmetry: at \( z = 2 \) the brake is 0.1353 and at \( z = -2 \) precisely its inverse (7.3891) — which is why \( \sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z) \).

blocks.caption: exploring exp() with NumPy
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

print('e           :', round(np.e, 5), '   <- Euler number')
print('exp(0)      :', np.exp(0))
print('exp(1)      :', round(np.exp(1), 5), '   <- equals e itself')
print('exp(-1)     :', round(np.exp(-1), 5))
print('1 / exp(1)  :', round(1/np.exp(1), 5), '   <- same! exp(-z) = 1/exp(z)')
print()
for z in [-5, -2, 0, 2, 5]:
    rem = np.exp(-z)
    sigma = 1 / (1 + rem)
    print(f'z = {z:>2}   exp(-z) = {rem:8.4f}   sigma = {sigma:.4f}')

blocks.html: Why e and not 10 or 2? e is the only base for which the slope of \( b^x \) is exactly \( b^x \) itself. As a result the derivative of the sigmoid is remarkably tidy: \( \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,(1 - \sigma(z)) \) — the derivative can be built from the function value alone. One reason gradient descent on logistic regression flows so smoothly.

The S-curve wasn't invented for machine learning — it is the universal shape of anything that starts slowly, accelerates and then saturates. A probability that cannot leave [0, 1], a population that cannot grow forever, a market that doesn't adopt everything at once: always the same sigmoid. Conversely, that is exactly why the function is so suited as a translation layer from 'arbitrary score' to 'probability'.

rows: turns the raw model output into a probability — the engine behind predict_proba() (this chapter)
classic activation of a neuron; in the output layer it delivers a probability per node. The MLP (multilayer perceptron) was originally built on it
relatives: tanh(z) = 2σ(2z) − 1 maps to (−1, 1); softmax generalises to multiple classes — see Multi-class
tames overconfidence: extreme scores are flattened into realistic, usable probabilities
logistic growth: populations start slowly, accelerate and saturate at the carrying capacity of their environment
adoption curves of new technology and products almost always follow the S-shape
squashes signals into a bounded range, for instance as a gate or squashing function

blocks.html: For the ML world the most important kinship is with tanh and softmax. Tanh is literally the same S-curve, stretched to (−1, 1) — handy when a neuron must be able to signal 'negative'. Softmax is the multi-class generalisation: it assigns each class a share of the total (all probabilities sum to 1). You can verify the kinship yourself with the code below.

blocks.caption: sigmoid properties and the tanh relation
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# symmetry: sigma(-z) = 1 - sigma(z)
print('sigma(-2)   :', round(sigmoid(-2), 4))
print('1 - sigma(2):', round(1 - sigmoid(2), 4), '   <- equal!')
print('sigma(0)    :', sigmoid(0), '   <- exactly 0.5')
print()

# tanh = stretched sigmoid: tanh(z) = 2*sigma(2z) - 1
for z in [-1.5, 0.0, 1.3]:
    print(f'z = {z:>4}: tanh(z) = {np.tanh(z):7.4f}   '
          f'2*sigma(2z)-1 = {2*sigmoid(2*z)-1:7.4f}')

blocks.html: In modern networks ReLU-style activations are often faster and more popular on hidden layers, but in the output layer for binary classification the sigmoid remains the standard to this day — for exactly the same reason as in logistic regression: it is the cleanest translation of a score into a probability.

In scikit-learn, decision_function is precisely the raw model output, and predict_proba the sigmoid of it. You can verify this yourself: compute the sigmoid of the raw output by hand and compare it with what predict_proba gives — identical. An extra insight from the course: with 2 features you have 2 coefficients, while the direction of a line needs only one number. The ratio of the coefficients gives the direction of the boundary, the magnitude gives your confidence level. Regularisation therefore changes not only the certainty but often also the orientation of the boundary.

blocks.caption: Manual sigmoid vs. predict_proba
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

i = 12
raw = lr.decision_function([X[i]])[0]
print('raw model output   :', round(raw, 4))
print('sigmoid(raw)       :', round(sigmoid(raw), 4))
print('predict_proba      :', lr.predict_proba([X[i]])[0].round(4))
prob = sigmoid(raw)
print('predict            :', lr.predict([X[i]])[0],
      '(probability', '> 0.5)' if prob > 0.5 else '(probability < 0.5)')

blocks.html: A hard prediction is simply the question "is sigmoid(raw) > 0.5?" — which is the same as "is the raw output positive?" Everything falls back on the prediction equation of chapter 2.
